course_description:
This course explores the complex but fascinating interactions that occur between humans and wildlife species and how these relationships can be better managed to ensure coexistence. Using local, national and international case studies of human wildlife conflicts, students will develop an in-depth knowledge of both the ecological and sociological issues underpinning the conflict. Through a series of lectures and workshops students will also be given knowledge and skill sets that allow them to not only equitably assess both sides of human wildlife conflicts but help them construct and deliver management plans and facilitate conflict resolutions. Topics to be covered include the diverse perspectives from which wildlife is viewed in different societies, the role of policy and legislation in the protection of wildlife, specific urban, regional and rural examples of human wildlife conflict, zoonoses, wildlife utilisation and feral pest management.

This course was last offered in external mode in 2025.

Management of human-wildlife interactions (HWIs) is considered to be one of the most challenging tasks for wildlife management practitioners around the world. Human-wildlife conflicts and resource competition imply costs on human social, economic or cultural life and on the ecological, social or cultural life of wildlife concerned, often to the detriment of conservation objectives and socio-economic realities. During this course, participants will learn about the human-wildlife interactions in regional, national and international settings, how these conflicts are managed, and how ideal conflict management strategies can be developed.

Like all real-world problems, addressing human-wildlife interactions requires transdisciplinary thinking and combining knowledge in new and interesting ways. We will explore theoretical frameworks for approaching human-wildlife interactions that go beyond disciplinary boundaries and provide a more holistic approach to better equip conservationists and other professionals in dealing with the issue. Dr. van Bommel blends scientific evidence of several academic disciplines (e.g., ecology, wildlife management, sociology, policy sciences, economics) and 20 years of real-world experience to help participants develop a deep understanding of human-wildlife interactions and will equip them with the practical skills necessary to develop human-wildlife conflict management strategies.

Using a variety of teaching and learning methods, students will learn about issues involved in determining and analysing human-wildlife interactions, and planning, implementing and evaluating conflict mitigation or prevention schemes. While the course covers theoretical components, it takes a very practical and pragmatic approach to management of human-wildlife interactions.

At the School of Agriculture and Food Sustainability, we are committed to creating an inclusive and empowering learning environment for all students. We value and respect the diverse range of experiences our students bring to their education, and we believe that this diversity is crucial for fostering a rich culture of knowledge-sharing and meaningful exploration. We hold students and staff accountable for actively contributing to establishing a respectful and supportive learning environment.

Bullying, harassment, and discrimination in any form are strictly against our principles and against UQ Policy, and will not be tolerated. If you have any concerns about your experience in this course, we encourage you to tell a member of the course teaching team. Your well-being and a positive learning atmosphere are of utmost importance to us.

course_aims:
The course aims to develop participant knowledge, understanding and skills to:

1) critically engage with theoretical questions and practical challenges posed by human-wildlife conflicts (HWIs).

2) understand, construct and deliver human-wildlife interaction management plans in many contexts and facilitate resolution.

learning_outcomes.description: Apply Conflict Management Strategies in HWIs: Understand the three levels of conflict and the different conflict management processes, and apply this knowledge to develop practical strategies for managing human-wildlife conflicts effectively.

Apply Stakeholder Engagement Strategies in HWIs: Understand the systemic properties of human-wildlife interactions, and apply this knowledge to engage effectively with various stakeholders to move conflicts towards coexistence.

Apply Knowledge in HWIs: Understand the role of different types of knowledge in human-wildlife interactions, apply this understanding to identify the politicization of knowledge, and recognize how the involvement of experts and their expertise can influence conflict dynamics.

Apply Financial Incentives for Conservation: Understand the role of financial incentives in managing human-wildlife interactions on private land and apply this knowledge to evaluate different economic tools, such as wildlife utilisation and market-based conservation efforts, to support sustainable land management practices.

Apply Policy Frameworks in Human-Wildlife Conflict Management: Understand the role of policy in managing human-wildlife conflicts, and apply this knowledge to evaluate different policy instruments and their effectiveness in mitigating conflicts between humans and wildlife.

Apply Evaluation Techniques in Human-Wildlife Interaction Management: Understand the role of evaluation in managing human-wildlife interactions, and apply this knowledge to develop and use evaluation questions, indicators, and data collection methods to assess the effectiveness of management strategies.

Integrate knowledge: Integrate knowledge from ecological, social, and economic disciplines to develop comprehensive management strategies that are ethical, sustainable, and effective at multiple levels of human-wildlife conflict.

assessment_details.task_description: This assessment requires students to participate in a multi-stakeholder mediation simulation focused on a fictionalized human–wildlife conflict in Belize. Students will be assigned stakeholder roles and participate in a facilitated Townhall-style negotiation and mediation process. The simulation is designed to expose students to the complexity of conservation conflicts involving competing values, identities, livelihoods, governance priorities, conservation objectives, and social tensions. These sequential assessment components intertwine with the mediation simulation assessment. Stakeholder Position Statement (10%) Due: Prior to the mediation simulation Length: ~1,000 words (individual) Submission : Turnitin Students will prepare an individual stakeholder position statement based on their assigned role in a simulated human–wildlife conflict. The submission consists of a written position statement and a stakeholder spider diagram that maps the key factors influencing the stakeholder's perspective. Drawing on the simulation materials and relevant course concepts, students will analyse their stakeholder's positions, interests, values, needs, objectives, relationships with other stakeholders, and desired outcomes from the mediation process. The spider diagram will visually represent the interconnected factors shaping the stakeholder's perspective and priorities. Acknowledging and/or referencing AI use Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Translation (MT) are emerging tools that may support students in completing this assessment task. Students may appropriately use AI and/or MT in completing this assessment task. Students must clearly acknowledge any use of AI or MT in each instance. A failure to acknowledge generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. The use of AI or MT must be acknowledged appropriately. Please see assessment guidelines in blackboard course site for specific instructions. Students may also refer to Library guides found under Additional assessment information > Acknowledging and referencing AI use. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Reflective Analysis (10%) Due: After the mediation simulation Length: ~1,500 words (individual) Submission : Turnitin Following the simulation, students will prepare a report for the members or constituents of their assigned stakeholder group, reflecting on the mediation process and its outcomes. The report should explain how the negotiation unfolded, evaluate the extent to which the stakeholder's interests and objectives were addressed, and critically analyse the process using relevant concepts and theories from the course, including but not limited to the levels of conflict framework. Students may discuss: how stakeholder positions, interests, values, identities, and needs shaped the negotiation; moments of conflict escalation, misunderstanding, collaboration, and learning; the role of evidence and knowledge in shaping stakeholder perspectives and decision-making; the role of policy, power, and procedural fairness in influencing the process and outcomes; the effectiveness and limitations of negotiation and mediation approaches; the extent to which the mediation generated acceptable outcomes for their stakeholder and opportunities for future collaboration; and the future steps that their stakeholder should take to advance their interests while contributing to constructive dialogue and long-term coexistence. Students should support their reflections using relevant course concepts and academic literature. assessment_details.title: Mediation Simulation
assessment_details.task_description: This assessment requires students to participate in a multi-stakeholder mediation simulation focused on a fictionalized human–wildlife conflict in Belize. Students will be assigned stakeholder roles and participate in a facilitated Townhall-style negotiation and mediation process. The simulation is designed to expose students to the complexity of conservation conflicts involving competing values, identities, livelihoods, governance priorities, conservation objectives, and social tensions. This assessment intertwines with the sequential position statement and reflection. Students must participate in the simulation to receive a mark for this assessment task. This assessment task is not eligible for re-mark because it is completed live during the scheduled class activity and cannot be replicated after the event. Due to the structure of the assessment, recording student performance is not possible. As there is insufficient reviewable evidence to reconsider the original assessment judgement, students cannot apply for a re-mark. Mediation Simulation Participation Students will participate in class in a facilitated multi-stakeholder mediation simulation involving negotiation, dialogue, conflict management, and media engagement. Students are expected to actively represent the perspectives, interests, and concerns of their assigned stakeholder group while engaging constructively with other participants. The simulation will involve: stakeholder caucus discussions, negotiation and mediation processes, responses to escalating tensions, engagement with contested evidence and competing narratives, and interaction with media representatives. This assessment task is to be completed in-person. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Read full task description Hide full task description

This assessment intertwines with the sequential position statement and reflection. Students must participate in the simulation to receive a mark for this assessment task. This assessment task is not eligible for re-mark because it is completed live during the scheduled class activity and cannot be replicated after the event. Due to the structure of the assessment, recording student performance is not possible. As there is insufficient reviewable evidence to reconsider the original assessment judgement, students cannot apply for a re-mark. Mediation Simulation Participation Students will participate in class in a facilitated multi-stakeholder mediation simulation involving negotiation, dialogue, conflict management, and media engagement. Students are expected to actively represent the perspectives, interests, and concerns of their assigned stakeholder group while engaging constructively with other participants. The simulation will involve: stakeholder caucus discussions, negotiation and mediation processes, responses to escalating tensions, engagement with contested evidence and competing narratives, and interaction with media representatives. This assessment task is to be completed in-person. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted.
